title: Cohort thermograph: end-to-end trace profiling and stage temperature map
content:
Purpose

Quick working notes for a new way of visualizing end-to-end latency: a "thermograph" that maps stage-level "temperature" (ms concentration and variability) across user cohorts. Goal is to identify which cohorts and stages contribute most to p95/p99 tail mass and to prioritize low-effort mitigations.

Background / motivation

We've been seeing repeated p99 regressions on the hosted fleet that are hard to root-cause from single-trace waterfalls. Many traces share similar signatures but differ by prompt prefix, conversation history size, and encoder-token-count. Rather than one-off trace hunts, the thermograph approach aggregates traces into cohorts and shows a per-stage heat intensity (centroid + variance) so we can prioritize high-impact stages across cohorts.

Cohort definitions used for this pass

- short-system: system prompt <= 80 chars, user prompt <= 160 chars, seqlen <= 512
- long-context: conversation history > 2k tokens OR recent-context appended > 1024 tokens
- embed-heavy: request includes embedding pre-compute hooks (reranker pipeline attached)
- cold-kv-miss: first request after model spin-up + KV cache miss (identified by kv_miss flag in trace)

Sampling and telemetry

- Time window: 2026-01-12T00:00 -> 2026-01-17T23:59 (5 days)
- Sample size: 18k traces total; cohort breakdown: short-system 9.4k, long-context 4.1k, embed-heavy 2.2k, cold-kv-miss 2.3k
- Instrumentation: per-stage timestamps from trace spans: ingress.receive, routing.match, env.setup, model.warmup, kv.lookup, batch.wait, model.generate, postprocess.emit, egress.send
- Derived fields: stage_duration_ms, start_offset_ms, kv_miss (boolean), seqlen_tokens (int), batch_size_at_exec

High-level aggregated latency (rounded ms)

- short-system: p50 98ms, p95 267ms, p99 447ms
- long-context: p50 186ms, p95 542ms, p99 1210ms
- embed-heavy: p50 142ms, p95 398ms, p99 772ms
- cold-kv-miss: p50 210ms, p95 920ms, p99 1785ms

Per-stage centroid and p95 contributors (short-system vs long-context)

short-system (p95 267ms) - median stage breakdown (centroid ms | p95 ms contribution):
- ingress.receive: 6 | 12
- routing.match: 8 | 20
- env.setup: 12 | 28
- kv.lookup (hit): 6 | 12
- batch.wait (mean queued): 30 | 70  <-- accounts for ~26% of p95 
- model.generate (tokens emit portion): 180 | 250 <-- dominant contributor to median and tail
- postprocess.emit: 5 | 10
- egress.send: 3 | 5

long-context (p95 542ms) - median stage breakdown:
- ingress.receive: 8 | 18
- routing.match: 9 | 22
- env.setup: 18 | 45
- kv.lookup (partial miss / extended): 22 | 110 <-- larger variance, common p99 driver
- batch.wait (larger effective batch sizes): 40 | 95
- model.generate (longer seqlen, kv fetch stalls): 360 | 710 <-- largest tail mass for long-context cohort
- postprocess.emit: 7 | 12
- egress.send: 6 | 10

Observations / pattern fingerprints

1) Two p99 phenotypes recur in long-context and cold-kv-miss cohorts:
   - phenotype A: extended kv.lookup stall (several redis calls chaining) -> model.generate starts late -> p99 dominated by kv lookup + token emission overlap. Signature: kv.lookup span with >100ms tail and a model.generate start_offset >200ms.
   - phenotype B: large batch.wait caused by burst alignment + seqlen heterogeneity -> model.generate inflated due to larger decode steps. Signature: batch.wait span >250ms and exec batch_size >= 16 for that slot.

2) For short-system cohort, batch.wait is unexpectedly a big chunk of p95 (26%). Hypothesis: small requests are being coalesced into medium batches when parallelism dips, causing waiting without significant generation amortization.

3) Cold-kv-miss cohort shows classic spin-up + cache-miss amplification: env.setup + model.warmup + repeated kv miss -> p99 >> other cohorts. Many of these are single-digit QPS tenants that hit dedicated cold paths.

Micro-hypotheses with quick tests (ranked by expected effort)

H1 (low effort): Reduce batch wait window for short-system cohort routes during low load. Test: roll a 6ms cap on batching window for route group r-sys-small for 3 hours on staging. Metric: p95 short-system should drop by ~20-30ms; monitor throughput and CPU. Linked: GH PR #5123.

H2 (medium effort): Parallelize KV lookups for long-context when seqlen_tokens > 1024 (split redis calls into a parallel fan-out). Test: synthetic replay of 5000 traces with forced kv_miss pattern. Metric: reduction in kv_lookup p95 and shift of p99 mass away from kv stage.

H3 (higher effort): Introduce predictive cache-probing for conversation-history tokens (pre-warm likely keys on open of a conversation). Test: feature-flagged rollout to 2% tenants; evaluate cold-kv-miss p99.

Quick experiments run so far (notes)

- Batching window cap experiment (staging, 4 hours): applied 6ms cap for r-sys-small. Result: short-system p95 dropped from 267->238ms (11% reduction). CPU unaffected. Some increase in small-model execs per second observed. Next: consider lowering to 4ms during <10qps windows.
- KV parallel lookup PoC (local): microbench shows parallel fan-out reduces worst-case kv_lookup latency from 160ms->48ms at high concurrency, but increases RPS to Redis and needs rate-limiting. Not safe to roll without quota controls.

Action items / next steps

- (Asha) Draft canary for batching-window cap on staging for 24h with real traffic capture (ticket JIRA-OPS-347).
- (Li) Build a telemetry flag to mark traces that used parallel-kv path for easier toggled rollouts.
- (Miguel) Run a targeted replay for 50 tenants who showed cold-kv-miss to reproduce phenotype A in perf lab. Capture flamegraphs for redis client.
- (Jonah) Add cohort thermograph view to the observability dash: x-axis stage, y-axis cohort, heat = p95 stage_duration_ms; include p50/p95/p99 tri-line. Minimal mockup attached in PR #5123.

Notes on visualization design (for subsequent handoff to observability team)

- Each cohort row shows three columns: centroid(ms), p95(ms), p99(ms). Each stage represented as stacked segments where width=centroid, color intensity scales with variance (stddev) and hatch for KV misses. Hover tooltip shows sample trace ids and typical signatures (e.g., batch.wait > Xms).
- Add a small-sparkline of batch_size_at_exec distribution per cohort to capture burstiness correlation.

Open questions / risks

- Does reducing batching window increase per-token cost materially for small models? Need cost simulation for 24-hour roll.
- Parallel KV increases DB TPS; need to coordinate Redis cluster quotas. Risk of moving p99 from KV to model.generate if underprovisioned.

Appendix: representative trace snippets (anonymized)

Trace A (long-context, p99):
- total 1872ms
- kv.lookup: 118ms (p95 span 112ms, p99 502ms due to tail retry)
- batch.wait: 92ms
- model.generate: 1460ms (start_offset 230ms)

Trace B (short-system, p95 sample):
- total 256ms
- batch.wait: 64ms (queued 6ms avg per slot)
- model.generate: 180ms

Trace C (cold-kv-miss, p99):
- total 1785ms
- env.setup: 230ms
- model.warmup: 380ms
- kv.lookup: 320ms (sequential retries)
- model.generate: 640ms

If useful, I can export a CSV of cohort-stage aggregates for the obs team and mock up the thermograph SVG – want the obs sprint PR?

-- end of notes --
